# Connection: Synced Config Must Be Host-Agnostic

## The Connection

Four documented failures share one shape: a config file specified an executable reference valid on the machine where it was written, and broke on the machine where it ran. On 2026-09-19, `~/.claude/settings.json` — synced across Mac and Windows via the `erash11/dotclaude` repo — carried a `PreToolUse` hook pointing at `/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/dcg`, which errored on every Bash/PowerShell call on Windows and double-executed on the Mac ([[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]]). On 2026-05-13, GSD generated hook commands in PowerShell call-operator syntax because it observed the user's interactive shell, but Claude Code executes hooks through bash on every platform ([[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]). On 2026-04-14, a hook invoking bare `uv` failed because the hook runner's PATH omitted `~/.local/bin` ([[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]). On 2026-06-11, Windows Task Scheduler failed silently on `pwsh.exe` because scheduled tasks spawn with the machine-level system PATH only ([[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]]).

## Key Insight

The related pattern in [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]] explains three of these as *environment* problems: the executing process has a frozen, minimal environment that differs from the authoring shell. This article isolates a distinct axis the 2026-09-19 case exposes — the config file is **portable across hosts**, so the reference must be valid not just in a different environment but on a different *machine*, with a different home directory, a different username, and a different OS path grammar.

The two axes prescribe opposite-looking fixes, and conflating them is how the 2026-09-19 defect was introduced. The environment axis says: *be more specific* — replace bare `uv` with an absolute path, replace `pwsh.exe` with `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe`, because the runner's PATH cannot be trusted. The host axis says: *be less specific* — never hardcode `/Users/kristinarash/...`, because the other machine has no such user. The reconciliation is that the correct form is **`$HOME`-relative and existence-guarded**: `if [ -x "$HOME/.local/bin/dcg" ]` satisfies both, resolving without PATH and without naming a host. Someone had reached exactly that form on 2026-09-19 — and then left the unguarded original in place beside it, so the array ran both. The guarded variant is not an addition to a config; it is a replacement, and a hook array executes every entry it contains.

A second-order consequence unique to the synced case: the repository is the propagation channel for the defect as well as the fix. A host-specific path committed once reaches every machine on the next pull, and a local repair that is never committed is one pull away from being undone ([[concepts/scoped-commit-in-dirty-working-tree]]). Non-synced config fails on one machine; synced config fails on all of them, asymmetrically, with the loudest error appearing on the machine that did not cause it.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-19 (21:23): the `Bash|PowerShell` `PreToolUse` array held both `/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/dcg` and `if [ -x "$HOME/.local/bin/dcg" ]`. "On Windows the guarded one exits silently; the absolute Mac path errors every call. On the Mac both resolved, so dcg was running twice per call." — [[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]]
- 2026-09-19: the inert counter-case — `/Users/kristinarash/DEV` in `permissions.additionalDirectories` was deliberately left in place, "harmless on Windows, required on the Mac." A host-specific path is only a defect when the config *executes* it.
- 2026-05-13 (17:09): GSD emitted `& "C:/Program Files/nodejs/node.exe"` for a bash-executed hook; all 9 hooks required rewriting to plain `node`. — [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]]
- 2026-04-14: hooks had to call `~/.local/bin/uv` because "Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`." — [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]
- 2026-06-11 (16:53): Task Scheduler required the full `C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe`; bare `pwsh.exe` failed with no error. — [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]]

## Related Concepts

# Baylor Load Simulator: Vercel Deployment and Navigation

The Baylor Load Simulator app was deployed to Vercel production on 2026-04-14, fixing a server/client date-serialization bug along the way and adding persistent navigation between its `/reference` (Reference Card) and `/admin` (GPS Sync) pages. Active feature development continued into May 2026, including a Projected-vs-Actual comparison view and ongoing work to reconcile the app's data model with Catapult's real-world sync behavior.

## Key Points

- Neon (serverless Postgres) returns `practice_date` and `synced_at` columns as native JS `Date` objects rather than strings; these had to be serialized to ISO strings in the API routes before being passed to React client components.
- The Vercel project was not yet linked, so the MCP deploy tool could not deploy directly - `npx vercel link` had to be run interactively in a separate terminal first, as a one-time prerequisite.
- The `CATAPULT_TOKEN` value could not be pasted directly into chat (likely due to special characters); the workaround was to add it to `.env.local`, then have the assistant read the file and push the value to Vercel via the CLI.
- A persistent dark navigation bar was added to the authenticated layout, linking to the previously-unlinked `/reference` and `/admin` pages; it is hidden on `/login` and visible on all authenticated pages. A third top-level tab, `/comparison`, was planned on 2026-05-12 to surface the new Projected-vs-Actual comparison view (see [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]]).
- `.vercel/` remains gitignored per standard practice (the project link itself is not committed), and `CLAUDE.md` was updated with the simulator's architecture, known gotchas, and deploy commands for future sessions.

## Details

The Neon date-serialization issue is a reusable lesson beyond this one app: any Next.js project querying Neon (or other Postgres providers using the `pg`/`@neondatabase/serverless` drivers) should expect timestamp/date columns to come back as JS `Date` objects, which are not directly serializable across the server-to-client component boundary. The fix - explicitly converting these fields to ISO strings inside API routes before they reach client components - resolved the deployment-blocking error.

Two pages, the Reference Card (`/reference`) and GPS Sync (`/admin`), existed in the codebase but had no way to reach them from the UI; adding the nav bar made them discoverable. The GPS Sync panel is functionally complete but not yet useful in practice - it will only become "live" once Catapult has actual GPS data for the practice dates being tested, which ties this deployment to the broader, ongoing challenge of getting reliable Catapult data into Baylor Athletics' various tools. Outstanding work includes connecting GitHub auto-deploy (Vercel dashboard, Settings > Git, with root directory set to `simulator`) so future pushes to `main` deploy automatically without a manual CLI step.

A month later, on 2026-05-12, development resumed with a `ComparisonChart` feature overlaying projected vs. actual practice load on `/practices/[id]/compare`, plus a confirmed plan to promote it to a top-level `/comparison` nav tab (see [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]]). Building that chart surfaced a Catapult sync-aggregation issue - the same period type ("1 ON 1") appearing twice, non-adjacently, in a single practice's data - which the team chose to leave aggregated for now rather than redesign the sync model mid-season (see [[concepts/catapult-period-aggregation-sync-policy]]). ## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

# Baylor Professional Development Request Forms (FAST 2026, Databricks Dallas)

On 2026-10-03 two Baylor professional development request forms were finalized as PDFs on the Desktop — FAST 2026 at Texas A&M (Nov 13, $226.80) and the Databricks Data + AI World Tour in Dallas (Oct 14, $174.40) — together with a cover email to supervisor Erin requesting approval. The session's substantive moves were a content *rollback* (a rewritten "Reason for Attending" field reverted to its original wording and verified by reading the text back out of each PDF) and a routing decision: the email was saved as an unsent Gmail draft rather than sent, because the recipient address was inferred rather than confirmed and the connected mail account is personal, not institutional.

## Key Points

- **Both reason fields were rolled back to the original wording, then verified from the artifact.** FAST's rationale is player-tracking / sport business / human performance analytics tied to the football GPS and PFF work; Databricks' is governed data pipelines and AI apps on a lakehouse with hands-on Lakebase and Genie. Totals were unchanged by the rollback ($226.80 / $174.40). Verification read the text back out of each PDF rather than trusting the edit to have applied.
- **The email was drafted, not sent, on two independent grounds.** `Erin_Boyette@baylor.edu` was *inferred* from Baylor's First_Last pattern — it appears in no Gmail history and no local project note — and the connected Gmail MCP account is the personal `eric.rash11@gmail.com`, so a Baylor approval request likely has to be rebuilt in Outlook from the Baylor address.
- **The email existed only in chat until explicitly saved.** Asked where it was, the answer was that it had never been persisted; it was reproduced and then created as a Gmail draft with both Desktop PDFs attached via `gws` `+send --draft`, and pulled back from Gmail afterward to verify subject, body, and attachments.
- **An internal inconsistency across forms was flagged rather than silently resolved:** both forms state "None to date" for other professional development this fiscal year, which conflicts with an HPForum form listing an event on 6/15/26.
- **The work lives on the Desktop, not in a repo,** so the closeout produced no `STATUS.md` update; the handoff was written to `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-10-02-pd-request-forms.md` instead.

## Details

The rollback is the transferable element. A rewrite of the "Reason for Attending" text was produced, reconsidered, and reverted — and the revert was confirmed by extracting the text from each finished PDF rather than by trusting that the edit had been reapplied correctly. For a form that will be signed and submitted, the PDF is the artifact that matters; checking the generator's intent is not the same as checking the document. The same instinct governed the Gmail draft, which was read back from Gmail after creation to confirm that the subject, body, and both attachments had actually landed. In both cases the verification queried the layer that owns the final state.

The send decision records two distinct blockers that happen to point the same way. One is factual: the recipient address is a pattern-based guess, and sending an approval request to a guessed institutional address is a visible failure. The other is structural: the only mail account the tooling can reach is a personal Gmail, and a Baylor approval email sent from a personal address is the wrong artifact regardless of whether the address resolves. Holding the message as a draft keeps the composed text available while leaving both decisions with the user, who must confirm the address and then either send or rebuild it in Baylor Outlook. The remaining items are all human-executed: sign both PDFs (`...Professional Development Request Form_FAST 2026.pdf`, `...Databricks Dallas 2026.pdf`), register for both events (Databricks requires an application for Oct 14; FAST's priority deadline is Nov 1), and reconcile the "other PD this fiscal year" line if the 6/15/26 Global Human Performance Forum was in fact attended — a correction that would have to propagate to both forms *and* the draft.

# Skill Sync Drift: Untracked Per-Machine Copies and the Synced-Duplicate Rule

A portability check across the Mac/Windows Claude Code setup failed on `articulation-skill`, and the investigation produced two durable rules. The proximate state was an untracked, gitignored copy on each machine with a `"off"` override in `settings.json`; the root cause was that the skill had been *deleted from the skills repo* on 9/10 (commit `665e558`), after which each machine silently kept its own untracked copy that git can never sync. The resolution made it a single git-tracked copy in `~/.claude/skills`, and established that when a claude.ai-hosted skill duplicates a local one, the **claude.ai** copy is the one turned off.

## Key Points

- **Untracked-per-machine is the failure mode, not the symlink.** The first diagnosis blamed a Windows-only symlink into `~/.agents/skills`; the real cause was a repo deletion that left both machines holding private, unsynced copies. Anything git does not track cannot drift *visibly*, only silently.
- **A one-machine diagnosis of a two-machine problem is unreliable.** The initial fix — delete the symlink, drop the gitignore line, remove the `"off"` override — was invalidated by the user's correction that the skill also exists on the Mac: re-enabling the local copy there would have made the Mac list it twice alongside the identical claude.ai copy.
- **Synced-duplicate rule:** when a claude.ai copy duplicates a local skill, set the *claude.ai* copy to `"off"` (local wins), matching the four other `anthropic-skills:*` overrides. Disabling the local copy instead only makes sense on the machine where the local copy happens to be missing. The rule was recorded in Tier A skill-bloat memory *and* the repo handoff so the Mac would see it.
- **Skill descriptions carry a hard budget and a "Do not use" obligation.** `articulation-skill` gained an explicit exclusion clause (not for slide decks — use five-slides-generator or research-in-5; not for light copyediting) and its opener was shortened to land at 648 chars, under the ~650 limit. Third-party `impeccable` was deliberately left at 895 chars because an upstream update would overwrite any edit.
- **Reconciling a tracked file with an untracked twin requires removal first.** The Mac must `rm -rf ~/.claude/skills/articulation-skill` before `git -C ~/.claude/skills pull`, because git refuses to overwrite an untracked file; if the Mac copy holds unique edits, it must be backed up and merged deliberately.

## Details

The deletion-then-divergence sequence is worth naming because it inverts the usual intuition about version control. Removing a file from a synced repo does not remove it from the machines that already have it; it converts a tracked, comparable artifact into an untracked, invisible one on every host. From that moment each machine's copy evolves independently with no mechanism to detect the divergence — and the portability checker only noticed because the skill was absent from the repo while present in the filesystem. The fix is therefore not "re-add the override" or "fix the symlink" but re-tracking the artifact, which restores both machines to a single comparable source. The untracked state also explains why the first, filesystem-only diagnosis was wrong: a single machine's directory listing cannot distinguish "machine-local by design" from "orphaned copy of a deleted shared file," and the question "does this exist on the other machine?" has to be asked rather than inferred.

The synced-duplicate rule resolves an asymmetry that `settings.json` overrides create. An override that disables a *local* skill is correct only where the local skill exists; on a machine missing it, the override is either inert or actively wrong, and the user ends up with a per-machine settings file — exactly the condition that makes synced config unmanageable. Disabling the hosted claude.ai copy instead produces one statement that is true everywhere: local wins. Two incidental hazards were logged alongside. A `git pull` during closeout merged Mac-side `settings.json` changes, requiring all five `anthropic-skills:*` overrides to be re-verified afterward (they survived) — a merge of a settings file can silently alter behavior even when it reports success. And Windows could not write two Mac transcript files under the Proulx-PelvicFloor project slug ("Filename too long"), so those exist only on the Mac; nothing was lost, but the sync is not symmetric. Commits: skills `2ca8fbd`, dotclaude `751bbdd` + `576ed1b`, DEV `08d0642`, with closeout adding DEV `f63414e`, global-memory `589008a`, dotclaude `6cfbe9a`.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]] — The sibling defect in the same `settings.json`: a per-machine entry left in a synced file.
- [[connections/synced-config-must-be-host-agnostic]] — The general requirement this rule serves: one statement that is correct on every host.

# Folder-Driven Mod Loading: Generating the Load List Instead of Maintaining It

On 2026-10-03 the Claude Code mod loading mechanism was redesigned so that the `~/.claude/mods/` folder is the single source of truth and the load list is *generated* from it. The prior arrangement maintained the list by hand in three places — a Windows user environment variable, a line in the Mac's `~/.zshrc`, and prose claims in the README — while only the `mods/` folder itself synced through git, so any missed edit failed silently. Generating the list immediately exposed the drift: Windows had been loading only 6 of 8 mods, with `twin-copy-guard` and `config-encoding-guard` documented as loaded but never added to the environment variable.

## Key Points

- **A mod loads if and only if three derivable conditions hold:** it has a manifest, it has no `.disabled` file, and it passes `claude plugin validate`. Validation costs ~0.6 s per mod, so validating all eight on every sync is effectively free and is run unconditionally rather than cached.
- **Disabling travels through git.** The off switch is a committed `mods/<name>/.disabled` file, so a decision to disable a mod reaches both machines on the next pull instead of requiring a per-machine config edit — the specific failure the redesign removes.
- **Per-platform writers, same derived content.** Windows runs `mods-sync.ps1`, which writes the user environment variable directly because Claude Code starts without a shell profile; the Mac runs `mods-sync.sh`, which writes a gitignored, per-machine `~/.claude/mods/.loadlist` that `~/.zshrc` sources.
- **The sync is hooked into existing routines rather than scheduled:** `dev-sync` runs it after pulling `~/.claude`, and `closeout` runs it when a mod changed, each reporting a single line such as `mods: 8 loaded, 0 disabled, 0 invalid`. The README was rewritten to *describe* mods rather than claim which ones load.
- **The accepted trade-off is that any folder dropped into `mods/` goes live on both machines after the next pull** — which is precisely why validation and the `.disabled` convention are part of the design rather than optional hygiene.

## Details

The defect this replaces is a pure derivable-state problem: the set of loadable mods is fully determined by the contents of a synced folder, yet it was being restated by hand in three unsynced locations. Hand restatement of derivable state fails in one direction only — omission — and omission is invisible, because a mod that was never added to the environment variable produces no error, no warning, and no difference in behavior that anyone would notice without comparing against the folder. The two missing mods had been *documented* as loaded, so the documentation actively concealed the gap. Generating the list closed the loop in both directions: the list can no longer disagree with the folder, and the README no longer makes a claim that can go stale.

The platform split reflects a constraint already established in this environment, that a process's view of its environment is fixed at launch and that Claude Code on Windows starts without reading a shell profile. Windows therefore needs the value written into the user environment variable itself, with a terminal or application restart before it takes effect — the reason the session's handoff requires restarting Claude Code on Windows to pick up all eight mods, since the running session still held a scratch copy. The Mac takes the opposite route: a generated file read by `~/.zshrc` at shell startup, kept gitignored because its contents are machine-specific absolute paths even though the inputs are shared. Two implementation notes were recorded. macOS ships an older bash, so one strict-mode line had to be removed from `mods-sync.sh` for compatibility, and the script has run under Git Bash but **not yet on the Mac** — the pending verification is `bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh` returning `8 loaded, 0 disabled, 0 invalid` after replacing the hand-written `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS` line in `~/.zshrc` with a conditional read of `.loadlist`. The work was also built directly rather than delegated to subagents, on the explicit judgment that it was too small to pay for delegation.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/claude-code-dev-mods-ui-bands]] — The mods this system loads; the 6-of-8 discovery is the first evidence of how they were actually being loaded.
- [[concepts/skill-sync-untracked-per-machine-drift]] — The same day's resolution of the same class of problem for skills: make the synced artifact authoritative instead of per-machine config.
- [[connections/settings-based-fixes-are-not-durable]] — Re-deriving on every run instead of capturing state, applied here to the load list.
- [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]] — Why the Windows environment-variable write requires a restart before it is visible.
- [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]] — The general class that restart requirement belongs to.
- [[connections/synced-config-must-be-host-agnostic]] — The host-portability requirement satisfied by committing `.disabled` rather than per-machine overrides.
- [[connections/derivable-state-should-be-generated-not-maintained]] — The cross-cutting pattern this redesign instantiates.

# Weekly Football Matchup Profiles (MatchupAnalysis_FB2026)

`MatchupAnalysis_FB2026` produces a weekly opponent profile from PFF EPA data, and on 2026-10-03 the Week 5 Baylor–Arizona State profile was generated alongside a Weeks 1–4 backfill. The read was unambiguous in direction and explicitly weak in confidence: ASU's run defense is elite (−0.409 EPA/run, 5th of 138) while its pass defense is merely average (−0.008), and Baylor's run game ranks 120th, so **Baylor has to throw**; ASU's offense ranks 127th and is worst through the air, pointing to a low-scoring game. The profile was flagged "trust lightly" because ASU had played only two FBS games and the previous week's Colorado pass-defense read had not held.

## Key Points

- **The directional conclusion and the confidence in it are reported separately.** A clean rank split (5th-of-138 run defense vs. average pass defense, against a 120th-ranked Baylor run game) supports a tactical read, while a two-FBS-game sample and a failed prior-week read bound how much weight it carries.
- **`pff_game_result.py --season-through N` is now the shared engine for mid-season and post-season analysis,** not just the backfill tool it was written as: Week 6's bye-week mid-season review runs `--season-through 5` plus Big 12 EPA standings, and the post-season version runs `--season-through 12` before the bowl.
- **Its drive-ending tables reconstruct the Week 4 23–13 final score exactly, which functions as a self-check** — a derived output that can be validated against a known ground truth each week rather than trusted on construction.
- **Two inputs are structurally unavailable on Windows.** The CFBD bundle (betting line, SP+, FEI, frozen prediction) cannot be produced because the API key lives only on the Mac, and PFF Ultimate tendencies require a browser — which is what blocks the Keys to Victory, leaving Weeks 3–4 ungraded for want of premium charting rather than for want of plays data.
- **The project lacks a charter,** so `slate-check` keeps flagging `Weekly_Matchups_2026` as DUE; writing one is an estimated five-minute fix.

## Details

The reporting discipline here is the durable part. A matchup profile is a forecast consumed under time pressure before a kickoff, which creates pressure to state a confident read; this one states the read and then names exactly why it might be wrong — opponent sample size, and a concrete prior failure of the same inference class the week before against Colorado. That pairing makes the artifact usable without being overtrusted, and it matches the broader practice in this environment of distinguishing a model's direction from its demonstrated reliability. The frozen-prediction element of the CFBD bundle is what would otherwise convert these weekly reads into a gradeable record, which is why its Mac-only API key is more than an inconvenience: without a pregame capture, the week's read cannot later be scored as genuinely out-of-sample.

The `--season-through N` generalization is a small but consequential architectural result. A script written to backfill prior weeks turned out to be the same computation the mid-season and post-season reviews need, differing only in the cutoff argument, so one engine now serves three cadences instead of three divergent scripts accumulating separate bugs. Its credibility rests on the drive-ending reconstruction: because the tables reproduce the Week 4 23–13 score exactly, a run that fails to reconstruct a known final is evidence of a data or logic fault rather than a judgment call. The open sequence after the ASU game is mechanical — re-pull data, run `pff_game_result.py --week 5`, write the result doc — while the Keys to Victory grader remains blocked on PFF premium charting access and the CFBD bundle remains blocked on being at the Mac. Commits: `5b4cafa` (Week 5) and `4c61641` (backfill).

# Python subprocess `text=True` Uses the Locale Encoding (CP1252 on Windows)

An independent verification pass on 2026-10-03 found that the `status-report` skill's PDF-height probe (`status-report/SKILL.md` line 336) called `subprocess.run(..., capture_output=True, text=True)` without specifying an encoding. With `text=True` and no explicit encoding, Python decodes the child process's output using the locale's preferred encoding — CP1252 on this Windows laptop — so Chrome's UTF-8 output failed to decode, `stdout` came back as `None`, and the regex applied to it then raised. The fix, confirmed resolved in a second pass the same evening, was to pass `encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"` explicitly.

## Key Points

- **`text=True` is not the same as "UTF-8".** It means "decode using the locale encoding," which on a default Windows install is CP1252 and on macOS/Linux is almost always UTF-8 — so identical code succeeds on one machine and fails on the other with no code difference.
- **The failure is displaced from its cause.** The decode error does not surface at the `subprocess.run` call; it surfaces later as a regex error on a `None` value, which invites debugging the regex rather than the decode.
- **`errors="replace"` was paired with the explicit encoding,** so a genuinely undecodable byte degrades to a substitution character instead of taking down the probe — appropriate for a scraped-output probe where approximate text is useful and a crash is not.
- **The same code block carried two further single-platform assumptions,** both flagged in the same pass: line 85 expected `~/.zshrc`-sourced credentials to be visible to Bash, and line 83 used `head -5`, which is Unix-only and not native to PowerShell.
- **The fix was verified statically, and the empirical check was explicitly left undone:** the optional run of the PDF-height snippet against curly-quote HTML on Windows remains an open confirmation item.

## Details

This belongs to a recurring family in which a framework's convenient default behaves differently than its name suggests, and the correct response is to state the intent explicitly rather than rely on the default. The parallel to Jinja2's `default()` filter not reliably handling `None`, and to openpyxl writing conditional-formatting fills with a transparent alpha channel, is exact: in each case the default produces plausible-looking code whose failure is silent or displaced, and in each case the remedy is an explicit guard or explicit parameter rather than a workaround at the point where the symptom appears. The specific lesson for cross-platform scripts is that any `subprocess` call capturing text output from a tool that emits UTF-8 — which is most modern CLI tooling, Chrome included — should name the encoding, because the default is a property of the host rather than of the program.

The surrounding findings make the broader point that a skill authored and exercised on one machine accumulates that machine's assumptions invisibly. Credentials sourced from `~/.zshrc` and a `head -5` invocation are both correct on the Mac and both wrong on Windows, and neither would be caught by reading the file on the machine where it was written. Only a deliberate pass asking "does this hold on the *other* machine?" surfaced them, which is the same move that resolved the skill-sync drift earlier the same day. The encoding fix was confirmed present on re-verification (`encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"`) while the two shell assumptions remained open, and the honest residual was recorded rather than closed: verification was static, so the probe has not actually been run on Windows against curly-quote HTML to demonstrate the decode path empirically.

# Claude Code Dev Mods: Prompt-Area UI Bands

On 2026-10-02, five Claude Code "dev mods" — plugin-style UI bands rendered above the prompt — were written, validated, and pushed (commit `7313dcd`) to streamline end-of-session and repo-hygiene workflow on the Windows laptop. All code was complete; **none of it ran**. Mod loading appeared to be gated behind a feature rollout: `claude -p --plugin-dir` and `claude plugin test` were both refused with "rollout switch served off," and in-session hot reloading was declined, so the mods remained unexercised and their tests had never executed. On 2026-10-03 the loading question was answered from the opposite direction — the mod set had grown to eight and Windows was in fact loading six of them, with two documented-as-loaded mods silently absent from the hand-maintained load list.

## Key Points

- **Five mods plus a next-steps panel:** `repo-band` (#1), `next-steps` (which absorbed the planned #2 resume buttons because both occupy the row above the prompt), `job-watch` (#3), `merge-cleanup` (#4), and `where` (#5). They live in `~/.claude/mods/` — not a session-scoped folder — so they persist and sync, with `mods/` added to the `.gitignore` allowlist in `~/.claude`.
- **Loading is controlled by a `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS` user env var**, which on 2026-10-02 listed five folders maintained by hand. By 2026-10-03 the inventory was eight mods, and generating the list from the folder revealed that `twin-copy-guard` and `config-encoding-guard` were documented as loaded in the README but had never been added to the variable — Windows was loading 6 of 8. The hand-maintained list was replaced by a generated one (see [[concepts/mods-folder-driven-load-sync]]).
- **Suggestion buttons populate the prompt box rather than submitting.** Asked whether next-steps buttons should send immediately as in the demo video, the choice was explicitly "give me the chance to edit."
- **"All the code is written and pushed" was rejected as "complete."** Since nothing had run, the honest status is code-complete-but-unverified, and the untested surface was enumerated: the Closeout and Closeout+exit buttons, the next-steps buttons, a real `merge-cleanup` branch deletion, and how `job-watch`'s status entry coexists with `statusline-command.py`.
- **Conservative-by-construction behavior:** `repo-band` uses read-only `git status` and never fetches (so it structurally cannot detect "behind remote"), scanning ~150 repos eight at a time, throttled to once per 20 s plus a 5-minute timer; `merge-cleanup` deletes only branches confirmed merged and worktrees with no uncommitted changes, and no-ops when `gh pr merge --repo` names a repo it cannot locate locally.

## Details

The design decisions share a common shape: each mod is built so that its failure mode is doing nothing rather than doing something wrong. `repo-band` forgoes fetching, which costs it the ability to report "behind remote" but guarantees it never mutates or stalls on network state across 150 repositories; the 8-at-a-time concurrency with a 20-second throttle and a 5-minute timer bounds its cost on a laptop. `merge-cleanup` encodes the existing post-merge-cleanup rule and refuses to act on anything it cannot positively confirm — unmerged branches, worktrees with uncommitted changes, or a repo named in a `gh pr merge --repo` invocation that has no local counterpart. The prompt-population choice for next-steps buttons is the same instinct at the interaction layer: a button that fills the box preserves a human edit point, whereas one that submits removes it. `job-watch` deliberately reuses `claude-stack-doctor`'s existing sources — Windows scheduled tasks under `\Eric\` and Mac launchd `com.keystone.*` — rather than defining a second inventory of jobs to drift out of sync.

Several implementation facts were learned that are independent of these particular mods. Bash heredocs collapse double backslashes to single, which mangles regexes in generated files — the Edit tool is the correct instrument for any content containing escapes. The plugin validator requires helper functions taking `$` to be declared at the top level of the file, forcing `refreshSoon` to be hoisted. A `grep` that finds no matches exits 1, which is not a type-check failure and should not be read as one. Background task notifications arrive at `prompt.submit` with `origin.kind = 'task-notification'`, which is both the mechanism `job-watch` uses to surface them and the reason `next-steps` must filter them out. Separately, the `dcg` `PreToolUse` hook in `~/.claude/settings.json` carried a hard-coded Mac path; it was removed on 2026-10-02 — and found restored again by the next day's closeout snapshot, making it a recurrence rather than a one-time defect.

The honest-status discipline is the 2026-10-02 session's most durable output, and the following day supplied its vindication from an unexpected angle. The direct question "Are all the mods complete?" had an easy affirmative available — everything was written, validated, and pushed — and was answered no, because validation is not execution. When loading was finally examined on 2026-10-03, the real state was neither "blocked by a rollout switch" nor "all eight running" but a silent partial load that only became visible once the list was derived from the folder rather than asserted. The resulting handoff is still a verification plan rather than a completion claim: restart Claude Code on Windows so the regenerated `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS` is picked up (the 2026-10-03 session was itself still running a scratch copy), and report what appears above the prompt or paste any `<mod>: hooks module not loaded` line. The restart requirement is itself the familiar Windows constraint that a process's environment is fixed at launch.

- [[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]] — The hard-coded Mac `dcg` path removed during this work is another instance of that defect, and its reappearance the next day establishes recurrence.

# Cross-Platform settings.json: Duplicate dcg Hook from a Mac-Absolute Path

On 2026-09-19, a hook error fired on every `Bash` and `PowerShell` tool call on the Windows machine. The root cause was that the `PreToolUse` hook array matching `Bash|PowerShell` in `~/.claude/settings.json` contained **two** `dcg` entries: an original with a hardcoded macOS absolute path (`/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/dcg`) and a later-added guarded variant (`if [ -x "$HOME/.local/bin/dcg" ]`). The guard was added but the unguarded original was never removed, so on Windows the guarded entry exited silently while the Mac-absolute path errored on every call, and on the Mac both resolved and `dcg` ran twice per tool call. The fix was committed and pushed on 2026-09-23, four days later, after the defect had produced 49 `PreToolUse` errors in a single session. It then came back — twice.

## Key Points

- **A guard is only half a fix.** Adding a guarded variant of a hook command without deleting the unguarded original leaves both entries in the array; hook arrays execute every entry, so the broken one still fires.
- **The failure is asymmetric across machines.** On Windows the Mac-absolute path does not resolve and errors loudly on every matching tool call; on macOS both entries resolve, producing a silent double-execution rather than an error.
- **Recurrence is proven; the mechanism is not.** The `settings.json` history traced on 2026-10-03 reads `d59b4dd` removed → `e72c374` restored → `f17531c` removed → `9603eb4` restored, the last under the message "mac snapshot (closeout 2026-10-03)". Something in the Mac closeout path rewrites the Mac working copy with the hook present; what that is remains unidentified and is an open action item.
- **A remedy can be worse than the defect.** `WORKFLOW.md:217` recommended `git checkout -- settings.json`, which discards *all* unstaged settings edits rather than isolating the unwanted hook — destructive, and it does not address the root cause. It was replaced with targeted removal of the hook object.
- **Pulling the settings file is itself a behavior change.** A closeout `git pull` merged Mac-side `settings.json` edits, after which all five `anthropic-skills:*` skill overrides had to be re-verified (they survived) — a successful merge of a settings file can silently alter what loads.
- **The layering rule:** machine-specific hook paths belong in the guarded or `machine.md` layer, never in shared `settings.json`. Shared settings must contain only references valid on every host that pulls them.
- **Running sessions keep erroring until reload.** Sessions already open when the edit lands continue throwing the hook error; only `/hooks` or a full restart reloads settings.

## Details

The fix applied on 2026-09-19 was minimal: remove the unguarded entry, leaving one hook in that array. Validation confirmed the JSON parsed and all 22 top-level keys remained intact, with a backup written to `~\.claude\jobs\06c56c44\tmp\settings.json.bak-20260919`. A separate cross-platform artifact — `/Users/kristinarash/DEV` listed in `permissions.additionalDirectories` — was deliberately left alone: it is harmless on Windows (a path that simply does not exist) and required on the Mac, illustrating that not every foreign-looking absolute path in a synced settings file is a defect. The distinction is between a path that is *inert* when absent (an additional-directory grant) and one that is *executed* when absent (a hook command).

The commit was deliberately not made during the 2026-09-19 session because `~/.claude`'s working tree carried unrelated uncommitted changes, making a blanket `git add .` unsafe; see [[concepts/scoped-commit-in-dirty-working-tree]]. The deferral's stated cost materialized: the defect persisted across four more days and produced 49 errors in the 2026-09-23 session before being removed, pushed, and verified. By 2026-10-03 the picture had changed in kind rather than degree. Three removals and two restorations in the commit log establish that this is not a mistake that was made once but a loop: something reintroduces the hook on the Mac side, each removal is overwritten by the next Mac closeout snapshot, and the Windows machine pays for it with a per-tool-call error. Until the writer is identified, every removal is a temporary suppression — which is exactly why replacing the documented remedy mattered: `git checkout -- settings.json` would have discarded unrelated settings work while leaving the regenerating source untouched, converting a recurring annoyance into occasional data loss.

The generalized rule is a layering rule, not merely a syntax rule: machine-specific hook paths belong in the guarded or `machine.md` layer, and shared `settings.json` must be written to the lowest common denominator of every environment it will reach. This is the same shell-and-path class of hook fragility documented in [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]] (PowerShell syntax emitted into a bash-executed hook) and [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] (bare `uv` invoked from a hook whose PATH omits `~/.local/bin`). See [[connections/synced-config-must-be-host-agnostic]] for the generalization, and [[connections/settings-based-fixes-are-not-durable]] for why a repeatedly-overwritten file demands removing the generating condition rather than re-applying the edit. The stale-settings symptom also recapitulates the launch-time-snapshot pattern in [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]]: Claude Code reads `settings.json` when a session starts, so an in-flight session's behavior reflects the file as it was at launch, not as it is on disk.

# Power Query Formula.Firewall: Structural Fix Over Privacy-Setting Workaround

On 2026-10-02, a Power Query `Formula.Firewall` privacy error in `VB_Revised.xlsx` (the Volleyball_GRID workbook prepared for Baylor volleyball staff member Mike Wenger) was traced to a five-query structure in which `Kinexon Master` both read the raw-data folder *and* consumed results from four helper queries. The immediate remedy — toggling the workbook's "Ignore privacy levels" option — worked but was rejected as the real fix because the setting had already been flipped back off once, likely by a save or a rename. The adopted fix collapsed the five queries into a single self-contained `Kinexon Master` query, removing the condition the firewall reacts to rather than suppressing the reaction. On 2026-10-03 the fix was confirmed on the user's own machine and handed to Mike as paste-ready instructions, leaving only his laptop unverified.

## Key Points

- **The firewall trips on cross-source composition, not on any one source.** `Kinexon Master` mixing a direct folder read with results from four helper queries (Sample File, Transform File, Parameter1, Transform Sample File) is what the privacy firewall blocks; one self-contained query gives it nothing to block.
- **Per-workbook "Ignore privacy levels" is not durable state.** It can be reset by a save, a rename, or opening the file via a web route, and a user's *global* Excel privacy setting can override it regardless. For a workbook that moves between machines, a settings-based workaround is a recurring failure, not a fix.
- **The test was run with privacy checks on, plus a failing baseline,** and the global setting was checked first to rule out a vacuous pass. On 2026-10-03 the user's own Refresh All on the fixed workbook completed with no errors, which is the second independent confirmation.
- **The remaining unknown was handed over as a scripted check, not an open question.** `Volleyball_GRID\docs\mike-email-2026-10-02.md` tells Mike to close saved copies, open the file from Box > Kinexon > SandBox in desktop Excel, run Data > Refresh All, read `Ref` tab cell D2 for the local `Kinexon Raw Data` path, and reply with the result — and, if it errors, to screenshot and change nothing. `STATUS.md` was set to "awaiting reply."
- **A concurrent session had already merged the branch.** Told to "merge the branch," git history showed `fix/firewall-single-query` merged the previous afternoon as PR #2; no new merge was attempted and the branch was cleaned up locally and on GitHub. Checking repo/PR state before acting on a merge instruction is the generalized lesson.
- **Live-file discipline:** the shared Box copy is never written by tooling; the fixed workbook was produced locally and the user performs the upload and rename.

## Details

The session's governing judgment is that a defect which can be suppressed by a setting is not fixed by that setting when the setting itself is fragile. The evidence was direct: the Box copy already contained the identical query code from the 9/30 repair, so the only thing that had changed was the workbook-level privacy flag, which had reverted — most plausibly during a save or during the rename of `VB_Revised_.xlsx` to `VB_Revised.xlsx`. A fix whose correctness depends on a toggle that the normal file lifecycle resets will fail again on the next save, and will fail invisibly on a second machine whose global privacy preference differs. Collapsing to a single query changes the class of the problem: with no cross-query data flow inside `Kinexon Master`, the firewall has no composition to evaluate, so the privacy setting becomes irrelevant and is retained only as belt-and-suspenders.

The verification design is the second transferable element, and it addresses a specific way confidence can be fabricated. A privacy-firewall fix tested with the firewall bypassed proves nothing, so the run was executed with checks on; and a test that always passes proves nothing either, so a baseline was constructed that reproduced the original error. The pre-check of the *global* Excel privacy option guards the same property from a different direction. Residual uncertainty was then narrowed rather than asserted away: the user's own clean Refresh All on 2026-10-03 added a second environment, but the workbook has still never run on Mike Wenger's laptop, so the handoff converts that gap into a bounded, scripted report — one path to open the file, one command to run, one cell to read, and an explicit instruction to change nothing on failure. That phrasing matters for a shared live file: an untrained user improvising a fix is the likeliest way to lose the repair.

A third, smaller lesson came from the merge instruction. Acting on "merge the branch" without first reading git history would have produced a confusing no-op or a conflicting action, because another concurrent session had already merged `fix/firewall-single-query` as PR #2 the previous afternoon. When multiple sessions share a repository, the instruction describes an intent whose state must be re-read before acting. Two incidental frictions were also recorded: pushes in `Volleyball_GRID` and `project-triage` print `failed to delete .git/worktrees/...: Permission denied` from stale worktree folders — harmless noise, the pushes succeed — and the global `MEMORY.md` hit its 2,500-character cap, requiring four lines to be shortened before the volleyball thread could be added. A small factual correction was logged: the staff member's surname is Wenger, not Weger.

# Connection: Derivable State Should Be Generated, Not Maintained by Hand

## The Connection

Four findings from 2026-10-03 are the same defect at four different altitudes. The mod load list was restated by hand in a Windows environment variable, a Mac `~/.zshrc` line, and the README, while only the `mods/` folder actually synced — and Windows turned out to be loading 6 of 8 mods, with the two missing ones *documented as loaded* ([[concepts/mods-folder-driven-load-sync]], [[concepts/claude-code-dev-mods-ui-bands]]). `DEV/COMMANDS.md:21` said "two are off" while the nine-row table beneath it actually broke down as 6 scheduled, 1 on-demand, 1 disabled, 1 pending shutdown. `WORKFLOW.md:49` claimed global-memory was the "only thing" carrying memory between machines, contradicted by 308 tracked memory `.md` files in the `.claude` repo. And `articulation-skill` had been deleted from the skills repo on 9/10, after which each machine kept an untracked private copy that git could never reconcile ([[concepts/skill-sync-untracked-per-machine-drift]]).

## Key Insight

Each of these is a *hand-maintained restatement of state that is fully derivable from an authoritative source* — a folder's contents, a table's rows, a repo's file list. Restatement fails in one direction almost exclusively: omission. A mod never added to the list simply does not load; a row that changed status simply is not recounted; a second memory tier that appeared after the sentence was written simply is not mentioned. None of these produce an error, a warning, or any behavioral difference an operator would notice, which is why all four survived for weeks and were found only by a pass that regenerated or recounted from the source.

The documentation is worse than neutral in this failure mode — it is the concealing agent. The README asserting which mods load is what made the 6-of-8 gap invisible, because anyone checking would read the claim rather than diff the folder. The prose count "two are off" is what made the table's four distinct states look like two. Compression into a summary sentence is what dropped "pending shutdown" as a category separate from "off." So the remedy has two tiers depending on how cheap derivation is. When the source can be read programmatically, *generate* the artifact: a sync script that enumerates the folder, validates each entry, and writes the load list cannot disagree with reality, and the README stops claiming anything it would have to maintain. When generation is impractical — a prose paragraph describing a table — the discipline is to **recount from the source at audit time and never trust the sentence**, and to treat the summary as a derived artifact with its own correctness condition. The untracked-skill case shows the limiting case of the same principle: once an artifact leaves the authoritative source entirely, there is nothing left to derive from, and drift becomes undetectable rather than merely unnoticed.

## Evidence

- 2026-10-03 (14:25): "Windows was silently loading only 6 of 8 mods: twin-copy-guard and config-encoding-guard were documented as loaded in the README but never added to the env var. The documentation-vs-reality gap was invisible until the list was generated." The README was then rewritten to describe mods instead of claiming which load.
- 2026-10-03 (18:19): `DEV/COMMANDS.md:21` says "two are off," but the A1 table's nine rows are 6 scheduled / 1 on-demand / 1 disabled / 1 pending shutdown. Lesson recorded: "recount from the table rather than trusting the sentence," and "'pending shutdown' is a distinct state from 'off' — collapsing them is what produced the miscount."
- 2026-10-03 (18:16): `WORKFLOW.md:49`'s "only thing" claim about global-memory was false; 308 tracked memory `.md` files were found in the `.claude` repo. `COMMANDS.md:21` also claimed eight jobs "run on their own" while the table included disabled, retired, and on-demand entries, and `:29` offered `kickstart` for a ritual agent STATUS said was disabled.
- 2026-10-03 (08:44): root cause of the skill drift was a 9/10 repo deletion (`665e558`) after which "each machine kept its own untracked copy, which git never syncs. Untracked-per-machine is the failure mode."

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
